[UCLA cut its GIS librarian position in 2024. Demand didn't go with it.]{.lede}

Geography has consistently been DSC's single largest workshop constituency: 64 of the
roughly {{< var instruction.total_attendees >}} UCLA workshop attendees since 2020,
more than any other department.

Before the position was eliminated in 2024, DSC's GIS librarian handled
{{< var gis.consult_low >}} to {{< var gis.consult_high >}} booked consultations a
year (2021 to 2023) across Urban Planning, Public Affairs, Environment and
Sustainability, and Digital Humanities. They also co-taught a graduate Public Health
course, ran systemwide UC GIS workshops that reached {{< var gis.ucgis_2023 >}}
participants in 2023 alone, and managed key research datasets, including the LARIAC
aerial imagery acquired through the Archive's gift fund. That demand hasn't gone
away. DSC still fields GIS requests, just without the specialist capacity to meet
them.

Nationally, 81 of 187 Carnegie R1 institutions ({{< var gis.r1_pct_with_gis >}})
maintain a dedicated GIS librarian, rising to {{< var gis.top25_pct_with_gis >}}
among the top 25 R&D-spending universities. UCLA has the highest research
expenditure of any UC campus, yet is one of only two UC R1 campuses without one. The
other, Santa Cruz, spends a fraction of what UCLA does on research. (UCSF also lacks
one, but it's a health-sciences-only campus with no undergraduates, not a fair
comparison.) Lower-spending UC peers like Berkeley and San Diego both maintain
dedicated GIS staff.

Campus-wide, UCLA's ArcGIS Online platform, used across Geography, Luskin, Fielding,
Digital Humanities, Political Science, and Social Data Science, has over 7,100
accounts and more than 3,000 active users in the past year, per an OARC governance
report from December 2025. Without a designated administrator, it's now running at
over 200% of its licensed storage.
